hook_text: One of the best flood defences on Earth isn't made of concrete. It's a swamp.
clip_script: When heavy rain falls on a city, roofs, roads and paving send it racing into rivers within minutes. Engineers fight back with dams, walls and drains: hard engineering. It works, until a drain clogs with litter or a wall breaks. So geographers also use soft engineering: plant trees and grass so rain soaks in, and protect wetlands, nature's sponges, that soak up floodwater and let it out slowly. Then add warnings: yellow, orange, red. In April 2022 a cut-off low dumped over three hundred millimetres of rain on Durban in about a day. More than four hundred and thirty people died. Many lived on river banks and steep slopes, and many never got the warning in time. The lesson: concrete, sponges and warnings, together.
visual_style: A whiteboard city with rain arrows racing off concrete into a river, then a wetland soaking it up like a sponge; a dam and a drain; a three-colour warning bar; a map of the KwaZulu-Natal coast.
pacing: Surprise hook, compare two approaches, a real case to finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn how to beat floods.
